studies.name: Hunt et al. — Effectiveness of interventions for improving educational outcomes for people with disabilities in LMICs: A systematic review
studies.draft_uses: Full review findings: 28 studies, 18 skills-for-learning studies with 12 significant effects, literacy/cognitive/handwriting/numeracy effects described as large but low-study-count, moderately significant effect for conditions for inclusion, one significant teacher-knowledge study, no studies of built-environment accessibility or inclusive education policies, all-but-one studies rated low confidence
studies.latest_known: Published 6 February 2025, Campbell Systematic Reviews 21(1):e70016 (DOI 10.1002/cl2.70016). Search covered studies up to March 2022. No update, correction or superseding publication found as of November 2026.
studies.what_changed: No figures changed; this is the current and only full version of this review. The draft's figures (28 studies, 18 skills-for-learning studies, 12 significant, literacy/numeracy/handwriting/cognitive effects significant and large, moderately significant conditions-for-inclusion effect, single significant teacher-knowledge study, all-but-one low confidence) are consistent with the published text confirmed across ERIC, PubMed, Wiley, and LSHTM repository records.

studies.name: Saran, White & Kuper — Evidence and gap map of studies assessing the effectiveness of interventions for people with disabilities in LMICs
studies.draft_uses: Two claims drawn from this source: (1) the EGM 'provides a starting point for researchers, decision makers and programme managers…'; (2) most impact evaluations came from upper-middle income countries, with limited evidence from low-income countries, and a significant gap in study quality; (3) studies focus on 'fixing individuals' with fewer studies on infrastructure or institutions.
studies.latest_known: Original publication: Campbell Systematic Reviews 16(1):e1070, 9 January 2020. A corrigendum was published 12 July 2020 (Campbell Systematic Reviews 16(3), DOI 10.1002/cl2.1104) correcting the income-country distribution figures: 'over half (n=50) the impact evaluations come from lower-middle income countries' was corrected to 'almost half (n=50)…' and the upper-middle income country count was corrected to n=48 (not n=50), with low-income countries confirmed at n=9. A separate but related EGM cited as Saran, White & Kuper 2020, Campbell Systematic Reviews 16(9):e1111 (DOI 10.1002/cl2.1111) also exists and may be a broader or updated version; its relationship to e1070 could not be fully established from available sources.
studies.what_changed: The corrigendum changes the characterisation of the income-country distribution of impact evaluations. The draft states 'most impact evaluations came from upper-middle income countries' — but the corrected text establishes that lower-middle income countries (n=50) actually had the most impact evaluations, slightly ahead of upper-middle income countries (n=48), with low-income countries at n=9. The draft's phrasing ('most impact evaluations came from upper-middle income countries') reflects the pre-correction wording and is inconsistent with the corrected version, which shows lower-middle income countries as the most represented group. Additionally, a second EGM (e1111) by the same authors and year exists in the literature and may represent a distinct or updated map; the draft does not cite or acknowledge it, and its scope relative to e1070 is UNKNOWN.
